solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Lacking height, birds about to join 'V' in rising

indicators.note: lacking says a letter is missing from the game birds named next

parts.note: pheasants are game birds
re is Latin-derived for about, concerning
V is the symbol for the volt, the unit of electrical potential

explanation.surface: Flying low, a flock of birds is about to slot into V formation as they climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking height' removes H from PHEASANTS; the 'V' is expanded to the unit it stands for rather than used as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1381 English uprising led by Wat Tyler is a famous historical rebellion, and a rising is an armed revolt.

clue.text: IT equipment timed out initially, parking under tree

indicators.note: in a down clue, under places the parking letter below the rest

parts.note: a palm is a tropical tree

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letters of the two words timed and out

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A computer has timed out and someone parks under a tree to deal with it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small handheld computer is a piece of information-technology kit.

clue.text: Flying to dam, three choppers fully equipped for battle

indicators.note: flying suggests the letters scattered and rearranged

parts.note: choppers is slang for teeth

explanation.surface: Three helicopters fly to a dam, as if on a military operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying' rearranges TO DAM THREE into ARMED TO THE; 'choppers' means teeth, not helicopters.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone carrying every weapon possible, heavily armed and ready to fight.

clue.text: Frenziedly knocked up curry, ignoring beginning of recipe

indicators.note: ignoring says a letter is dropped from what precedes
knocked up, in a down clue, says the curry is written bottom to top

parts.note: a korma is a mild curry

indicators.note: beginning of takes the first letter of recipe

explanation.surface: Someone frantically threw together a curry without bothering with the recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked up' reverses KORMA to AMROK; 'ignoring' then drops R, the first letter of recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: To run amok is to behave wildly and uncontrollably, so the word works as an adverb of frenzy.

clue.text: Mickey Mouse beat Dumbo up

indicators.note: up, in a down clue, says the letters run upward, so read backwards

parts.note: to top is to beat or surpass
a nit is a fool, a dumbo

explanation.surface: Two Disney characters face off: Mickey Mouse beats Dumbo.
explanation.walkthrough: Mickey Mouse is British slang for second-rate, not the cartoon; 'up' reverses TOPNIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal adjectives for something trivial, shoddy and of little importance.

clue.text: Sent back bloodstained boxing glove, last in sale

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing what follows within the red

parts.note: bloodstained things are red
a mitt is a glove

indicators.note: last in takes the final letter of sale

explanation.surface: A bloodied boxing glove was the final lot in an auction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boxing' is a container signal, not the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Remitted can mean referred back or returned, as a case remitted to a lower court.

clue.text: Overthrown queen left guards

indicators.note: guards means holding something within

parts.note: someone who vanished has left

explanation.surface: A deposed queen fled, leaving her guards behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A defeated, conquered enemy has been overthrown.

clue.text: Much appreciate major bank in rest area

indicators.note: in places the middle pieces inside the rest area

parts.note: a lay-by is a roadside stopping place in Britain
major means great
a bank is a store or reserve

explanation.surface: A big bank sets up in a motorway rest area.
explanation.walkthrough: A LAY-BY is a British roadside pull-in for drivers to stop.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to value something highly, to set great importance on it.

clue.text: Relative lifting a drink, that's plausible

indicators.note: lifting, in a down clue, raises the a to the top of the relative

parts.note: a dad is a relative
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: A relative raises a drink in a toast that sounds about right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifting' moves the A of DAD to the top, making ADD.
explanation.definitionFit: Something which is consistent and makes sense is said to be believable in this idiom.

clue.text: Ridicule Geordie, perhaps, with no time for his community

parts.note: the Geordie lamp was a miner's safety lamp designed by George Stephenson

indicators.note: with no says a letter is removed

parts.note: the Toon is Newcastle, the Geordie's home town

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a Geordie for having no time for his own community.
explanation.walkthrough: A Geordie is a native of Newcastle, which locals call the Toon; 'Geordie' also names a miner's lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: To lampoon someone is to satirise and mock them publicly.

clue.text: Flash knight regarded as wealthy

parts.note: a mo is a moment, an instant or flash
N is the chess notation for knight
eyed means looked at, regarded

explanation.surface: A showy knight is seen as rich.
explanation.definitionFit: Having plenty of cash makes one rich, affluent.

clue.text: Trend from Shoreditch not totally revolutionary

indicators.note: revolutionary says the letters are turned round
from says the letters are taken out of the place name
not totally says only part of the word is used

explanation.surface: A trend coming out of trendy Shoreditch is not wholly revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: SHOREDITCH is a fashionable London district; 'revolutionary' reverses EDIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A tide can mean a general tendency or current of opinion, as in the tide of history.

clue.text: A drugs bust on base for soldiers

indicators.note: on, in an across clue, places the first part after the base

parts.note: the foot is the base of something

indicators.note: bust means broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Police carry out a drugs raid on a military base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' rearranges A DRUGS into GUARDS, not a police raid.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an infantry regiment group in the British Army, so its members are soldiers.

clue.text: Small shiner resulting from aggressive brawl according to Spooner

indicators.note: the Spooner reference says the opening sounds of two words are swapped

parts.note: lairy is British slang for loud, flashy and aggressive
a fight is a brawl

explanation.surface: A small black eye resulted from a violent brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: A shiner looks like a black eye but here is something that shines.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny decorative bulbs strung on Christmas trees are small things that shine.

clue.text: Prescribed drug, complain about gaining weight

indicators.note: gaining means taking in a further piece
about says the word is turned round

parts.note: to carp is to complain
oz, ounce, is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A patient complains about putting on weight while taking medication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses CARP to PRAC, which then takes in OZ.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the brand name of the antidepressant fluoxetine, available on prescription.

clue.text: One played Juliet with pressure, after he was playing Romeo

indicators.note: after puts the pressure letter last

parts.note: Juliet is J in the NATO alphabet

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are performed in a new order

parts.note: Romeo is R in the NATO alphabet
P is the symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: An actor played Juliet under pressure, having already played Romeo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges HE WAS into EWSHA.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small musical instrument twanged against the mouth, so something that is played.

clue.text: Half serving of bran added to grain of loaf

indicators.note: added to puts the half-word into the grain

parts.note: cereal is grain

indicators.note: half serving of takes the first half of the word bran

explanation.surface: A recipe adds a half-serving of bran to the grain in a loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf' is British slang for the head (use your loaf), so 'of loaf' means of the brain.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the brain, which slang calls the loaf; it also means intellectual.

clue.text: Counsellor recreating past times probing that man in regression

indicators.note: in regression says the assembled letters run backwards

parts.note: retro styles recreate the past

indicators.note: probing puts the times sign inside

parts.note: he is that man
X is the multiplication sign, times

explanation.surface: A therapist recreates past times by probing a man through regression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'probing' puts X inside HE; 'in regression' reverses RETROHXE.
explanation.definitionFit: One who urges and advises earnestly is a kind of adviser.

clue.text: Ripped physique without extremely hefty arms

indicators.note: ripped means torn apart, so the letters are rearranged
extremely takes the outer letters of hefty

explanation.surface: A ripped physique without very hefty arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes H and Y, the ends of hefty, from PHYSIQUE before 'Ripped' shuffles the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To arm is to equip with weapons, so both verbs mean to supply or fit out.

clue.text: Heard man is jet-skier?

indicators.note: heard says the word is spoken, a sound-alike

parts.note: geezer is British slang for a man

explanation.surface: Someone overheard that a certain man is a jet-skier.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the hot spring is commonly pronounced like geezer. 'jet-skier' reads as one who rides jet skis but means something that jets water skyward.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot spring that shoots water up into the sky is whimsically a jetting thing aimed at the sky.

clue.text: Poem working in a way, uplifted nation

indicators.note: in places the working word within the road

parts.note: Rd, road, is a way
on means working, operating

indicators.note: uplifted, in a down clue, says the letters read upward, so backwards

parts.note: UAE is the United Arab Emirates, a nation

explanation.surface: A poem at work in its own way lifts up a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a fixed verse form of thirteen or so lines with two rhymes and a refrain.

clue.text: Sweet and sour in starters of the Eastern eateries

indicators.note: in places the sour word inside the opening letters
starters of takes the first letters of the three words

parts.note: milk gone off is sour

explanation.surface: Sweet and sour dishes appear among the starters of Eastern restaurants.
explanation.definitionFit: A chewy confection of boiled sugar and butter is a sweet.

clue.text: Neglected jockey outflanked

indicators.note: to jockey is to manoeuvre, shifting the letters around

explanation.surface: An overlooked jockey was outflanked in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jockey' is a verb here, not the rider.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nobody mentions is ignored, unremarked and overlooked.

clue.text: Swallow sad, feathers not working

definitions.meaning: out of action, as a computer system

explanation.surface: A swallow is miserable because its feathers have stopped working.
explanation.walkthrough: Four separate definitions of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means to gulp, to be dejected, fine plumage and out of action.

clue.text: Plants with no uses for carnivore

indicators.note: with no says the following word is removed

parts.note: crocuses are flowering plants

explanation.surface: Plants with no uses are fit only as food for a carnivore.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for crocodile, a meat-eating reptile.

clue.text: Pawn book voucher

parts.note: P is the chess notation for pawn
a ledger is an account book

explanation.surface: A pawnbroker hands over a book voucher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pawn' looks like the verb to pledge, but it is the chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: One who vouches for something gives a promise or guarantee, so both nouns name a guarantor.

clue.text: Honey's regularly used in food of islanders

indicators.note: used in places the picked letters inside the food

parts.note: fare is food

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of the word

explanation.surface: Honey regularly features in the cooking of an island people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes O, E and S from Honey's.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of the Faroe Islands in the North Atlantic are called by this collective name.

clue.text: Strangled by tall youth at sea, Blackbeard should have been more careful

indicators.note: strangled by says the pirate is held tight inside
at sea means confused, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Edward Teach was the pirate known as Blackbeard

explanation.surface: A pirate captain throttled by a tall youth on the high seas should have been more careful.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence, but 'Blackbeard' is the wordplay piece, not the subject; the definition is the closing phrase alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a told-you-so remark to someone suffering for their own carelessness.
